## Creating a project

We'll build a small analysis project to work through the commands.
Make a directory and move into it:

```bash
mkdir penguin_analysis
cd penguin_analysis
```

Now create the project:

```bash
uv init --bare
```

```out
Initialized project `penguin-analysis`
```

The `--bare` flag says
"only create the `pyproject.toml`, nothing else".
That is what you want for a data analysis project.

:::{.callout-warning}
If you run `uv init` *without* `--bare`,
`uv` sets you up to build and publish a Python **package**.
It creates a `src/` directory, a `README.md`,
a `[build-system]` block,
and a git repository.

That is the right thing when you are writing a library
(see the [packaging chapters](1110-packaging.qmd) later in this book),
but it is a lot of scaffolding you do not need
for a folder of notebooks and scripts.
Start with `--bare` and add what you need.
:::

Let's look at the one file it made:

```bash
cat pyproject.toml
```

```out
[project]
name = "penguin-analysis"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = []
```

This is the file where your project **declares** what it needs.
Right now it needs nothing.

### Pinning the Python version

`requires-python` above says "any Python 3.14 or newer will do".
That is a rule for the *solver*.
It does not say which Python you are actually using.

To record the exact version this project is built with:

```bash
uv python pin 3.14
```

```out
Pinned `.python-version` to `3.14`
```

This creates a `.python-version` file containing a single line:

```{.default filename=".python-version"}
3.14
```

Commit this file.
It is what makes `uv` pick the same interpreter on your collaborator's machine
as it did on yours.

:::{.callout-note}
`.python-version` and `requires-python` have to agree.
If you ask for a pin that the `pyproject.toml` forbids,
`uv` will refuse rather than quietly do the wrong thing:

```bash
uv python pin 3.12
```

```out
error: The requested Python version `3.12` is incompatible with the project `requires-python` value of `>=3.14`.
```
:::

## Adding packages

Now let's add the packages our analysis needs.

```bash
uv add pandas palmerpenguins
```

```out
Using CPython 3.14.3
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Resolved 6 packages in 268ms
Downloading pandas (10.7MiB)
Downloading numpy (5.3MiB)
 Downloaded numpy
 Downloaded pandas
Prepared 5 packages in 2.02s
Installed 5 packages in 33ms
 + numpy==2.5.5
 + palmerpenguins==0.1.6
 + pandas==3.1.1
 + python-dateutil==4.0.0
 + tzdata==2026.6
```

Read that output line by line,
because a single `uv add` did four separate things:

1. **Found an interpreter** matching our pin (CPython 3.14.3).
2. **Created the virtual environment** in a `.venv/` folder inside the project.
   You never asked for this.
   `uv` makes it the first time you need it.
3. **Resolved** 6 packages.
   That count includes the project itself.
   We asked for 2,
   and the other 3 are dependencies of the ones we asked for.
4. **Installed** 5 packages, at exact versions.

And the project directory now looks like this:

```bash
ls -a
```

```out
.python-version
.venv
pyproject.toml
uv.lock
```

Two new things appeared, `.venv/` and `uv.lock`.
Our `pyproject.toml` also grew a `dependencies` list:

```{.toml filename="pyproject.toml"}
[project]
name = "penguin-analysis"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = [
    "palmerpenguins>=0.1.6",
    "pandas>=3.1.1",
]
```

Notice that `uv` wrote `>=` and not `==`.
It recorded "this project needs at least pandas 3.1.1",
because that is what was current when you asked.
If you need an exact version,
say so when you add it:

```bash
uv add "pandas==3.1.1"
```

Quote version specifiers.
An unquoted `==` happens to be safe,
but the shell reads an unquoted `>` or `<` as a redirect.
In Bash, `uv add pandas>=3.0.0` ignores the version you typed,
adds pandas with `uv`'s own lower bound (`pandas>=3.1.1`),
and leaves an empty file called `=3.0.0` in your project.
In zsh, the default shell on macOS, it stops with `zsh: 3.0.0 not found`.

:::{.callout-tip title="New since DSCI 521"}
For an analysis project,
this book declares exact versions for every package, not just one.
[uv: pinning exact versions](0545-virtual-environments-python-uv-exact-pins.qmd)
shows how to make `uv add` write `==` every time, and why.
:::

## The two files that matter

This is the most important section of the chapter.

`pyproject.toml` records what your project **asks for**.
`uv.lock` records what it actually **got**.

Open `uv.lock` in your editor and you will find something much longer
than the lines you wrote in `pyproject.toml`:

```{.toml filename="uv.lock"}
version = 1
revision = 5
requires-python = ">=3.14"
resolution-markers = [
    "sys_platform == 'win32'",
    "sys_platform == 'emscripten'",
    "sys_platform != 'emscripten' and sys_platform != 'win32'",
]

[[package]]
name = "numpy"
version = "2.5.5"
source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" }
sdist = { url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/4e/3a/.../numpy-2.5.5.tar.gz", hash = "sha256:..." }
wheels = [
    { url = "https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/6a/9a/.../numpy-2.5.5-cp314-cp314-macosx_10_15_x86_64.whl", hash = "sha256:..." },
    ...
]
```

Every package, at an exact version,
including the ones you never named,
with the URL it came from and a checksum of the file.
The lockfile covers every operating system,
which is why it lists a separate wheel for macOS, Linux, and Windows.
That is what lets one lockfile work for your whole team.

:::{.callout-warning}
This is also where the `pip freeze` file we saw in
[Virtual environments: Python (uv)](0520-virtual-environments-python-uv.qmd)
falls down:

```bash
pip freeze > requirements.txt
```

`pip freeze` writes down whatever happens to be installed in your environment
*right now*,
on *your* operating system,
with no distinction between the packages you asked for
and the packages that came along for the ride.
Send that file to someone on a different OS and it may simply not install.

`uv.lock` is not that.
It is generated from your `pyproject.toml` by a solver
that knows about all platforms at once.
This separation, declared versus locked,
is the whole point,
and it is the same idea as `renv.lock` in R.
:::

Both files get committed to git.
The `.venv/` directory does **not** get committed.
It contains hundreds of megabytes of installed packages
that `uv` can rebuild in seconds from the lockfile.

A minimal `.gitignore` for a `uv` project:

```{.default filename=".gitignore"}
# Python-generated files
__pycache__/
*.py[oc]

# Virtual environments
.venv
```

:::{.activity}
Which files should you commit to your repository when using `uv`?
(one or more correct answers)

- A. `pyproject.toml`, because it declares which packages the project needs
- B. `uv.lock`, because it records the exact versions that were installed
- C. `.python-version`, because it records which interpreter the project uses
- D. `.venv/`, because your collaborators need the installed packages
- E. Only `uv.lock`, since it contains everything in `pyproject.toml` anyway

:::

## Running your code

Here is where `uv` differs most from what you may have seen before.
You do **not** activate the environment.

Put this in a file called `penguins.py`:

```{.python filename="penguins.py"}
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins

penguins = load_penguins()
print(penguins.head())
```

And run it with `uv run`:

```bash
uv run penguins.py
```

```out
  species     island  bill_length_mm  ...  body_mass_g     sex  year
0  Adelie  Torgersen            39.1  ...       3750.0    male  2007
1  Adelie  Torgersen            39.5  ...       3800.0  female  2007
2  Adelie  Torgersen            40.3  ...       3250.0  female  2007
3  Adelie  Torgersen             NaN  ...          NaN     NaN  2007
4  Adelie  Torgersen            36.7  ...       3450.0  female  2007

[5 rows x 8 columns]
```

`uv run` does three things before it runs anything.
It finds the project by walking up from your current directory,
makes sure the environment matches the lockfile,
and *then* runs your command inside that environment.

You can confirm which interpreter you actually got:

```bash
uv run python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"
```

```out
/Users/dan/penguin_analysis/.venv/bin/python
```

That is the project's `.venv`,
not the system Python that `which python3` would have found.
On Windows the path ends in `.venv\Scripts\python.exe` instead.

This works for any command, not just Python scripts:

```bash
uv run jupyter lab
uv run quarto render
uv run pytest
```

Why Quarto needs `uv run` in particular has its own chapter,
[uv: rendering Quarto documents](0550-virtual-environments-python-uv-quarto.qmd).

:::{.callout-tip}
The reason to prefer `uv run` over activating an environment
is that it removes an entire category of bug.
There is no "which environment am I in?" question to get wrong,
and no half-remembered `activate` step
between you and a reproducible result.

You *can* activate the environment the traditional way
if some tool requires it:

::: {.panel-tabset group="shell"}
## macOS and Linux

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
```

## Windows (Git Bash)

```bash
source .venv/Scripts/activate
```

## Windows (PowerShell)

```powershell
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```
:::

But if you find yourself doing this often,
it is usually a sign that a `uv run` would have been simpler.
:::

### Running something once

Sometimes you want a package for a single command
and you do not want it in your project.
`uv run --with` installs it temporarily:

```bash
uv run --with cowsay cowsay -t "uv run --with is temporary"
```

```out
Installed 1 package in 2ms
  __________________________
| uv run --with is temporary |
  ==========================
                          \
                           \
                             ^__^
                             (oo)\_______
                             (__)\       )\/\
                                 ||----w |
                                 ||     ||
```

Afterwards, `cowsay` is not in your project's environment,
your `pyproject.toml` is unchanged,
and your lockfile is unchanged.
